title: Ekman v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Jurisprudential Evolution of Research and Experimental Expenditures: From the Character-Use Distinction in Ekman to the Contemporary Amortization Regime
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
subject: Section 174 Research Expenditures
summary: Ekman v. Commissioner, 184 F.3d 522 (6th Cir. 1999), holds that U.S. taxpayers cannot deduct the acquisition cost of depreciable property, such as a $7,000 Porsche engine used as a research testbed, as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174(c). The property's character, not its research-only use, controls, a principle the IRS applies to R&D credit supply QREs.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Case Identification and Procedural Posture

In the United States federal tax system, the boundary between currently deductible or creditable research expenditures and capitalizable asset acquisitions represents one of the most frequently litigated fault lines in research and development (R&D) tax controversies. The landmark appellate decision by the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit in Ekman v. Commissioner, 184 F.3d 522 (6th Cir. 1999), affirming the United States Tax Court's decision in T.C. Memo. 1997-318, 74 T.C.M. (CCH) 72 (1997), establishes a foundational precedent governing the tax treatment of tangible property acquired for use in experimental activities. Decided on June 4, 1999, following oral argument on April 22, 1999, the Sixth Circuit opinion—alongside the Tax Court's separate order denying litigation costs and its decision entered on February 4, 1998, which declared a $307 income tax deficiency for 1991 and denied the request for litigation costs—resolves critical questions regarding the statutory exclusion of depreciable property under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174(c), the definition of wear and tear under IRC § 167(a), and the threshold for recovering attorney's fees under IRC § 7430.
Factual Background and the Taxpayer's Claim

The controversy originated from the 1991 joint federal income tax return filed by petitioners-appellants Leonard Charles Ekman and Kaye Layne Ekman. From the evidence adduced at trial, it appeared that the standard Porsche 928 S4 engine was designed to run comfortably at speeds of 130 to 150 miles per hour, but it was not designed for racing. Beginning around 1984, Leonard Ekman initiated mechanical development work on a Porsche 928 S4 two-valve engine, operating on the commercial premise that a niche market existed for a vehicle powered by a modified version of this powertrain that would be adaptable for racing while still usable as a regular street vehicle. In late 1990, Ekman decided to intensify his engineering efforts and, after consultations with other mechanics familiar with the Porsche engine suggested that his concept would be more suitable for a four-valve engine, shifted his technical focus from a two-valve configuration to a four-valve configuration, purchasing a damaged Porsche 928 S4 four-valve engine for $7,000 in March 1991.

To execute his performance enhancement objectives, Ekman repaired the damaged engine and then made the modifications to enhance it himself; later in 1991 he enlisted partners in the venture under an agreement providing that the enhancement of the engine remained Ekman's own activity while the partners were to develop and produce other parts and components to complement the enhanced engine, and the expenses at issue included cam development, piston development, engine block development, and cylinder head development. Additionally, Ekman acquired two used Porsche automobiles that provided the parts and the body into which the $7,000 engine was placed after the engine enhancements had been completed. Crucially, the commercial objective of Ekman's venture was not to sell the specific modified $7,000 engine as a finished good; rather, the engine served as an experimental testbed to validate engineering modifications that, once proven successful in increasing horsepower, could be replicated and commercialized across other Porsche 928 S4 engines. While Ekman succeeded technically in increasing the engine's horsepower, the tax dispute centered on how the underlying costs were reported on his 1991 return. On that return, the Ekmans claimed immediate research and experimental deductions under IRC § 174(a) for all costs associated with the camshaft, piston, cylinder head, and engine block development, as well as the $7,000 acquisition cost of the damaged Porsche 928 S4 engine itself.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue issued a notice of deficiency disallowing the entirety of the claimed R&D deductions. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) initially determined that all claimed expenditures—both the component development outlays and the engine acquisition cost—constituted capital expenditures for tangible assets that had to be capitalized and recovered through depreciation deductions under IRC § 167 once placed in service, rather than expensed immediately under IRC § 174(a).

Prior to trial in the U.S. Tax Court, following the taxpayers' production of substantiating evidence, the Commissioner conceded approximately 90% of the assessed deficiency, agreeing to allow the § 174 deductions for all component development expenses (camshafts, pistons, cylinder heads, and block modifications) except for the $7,000 claimed for the purchase price of the Porsche engine. At trial and on appeal, the Commissioner maintained that the $7,000 engine was a capital asset of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167, thereby barred from deduction by IRC § 174(c) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(b). In the alternative, the Commissioner asserted that the $7,000 outlay was barred by Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(3)(vi) as an expenditure for the acquisition of another's production, model, or process. When the Ekmans subsequently petitioned for $13,850 in litigation costs and attorney's fees under IRC § 7430 based on their pre-trial victory over 90% of the deficiency, the Commissioner opposed the petition, contending that the government's administrative and litigation positions were substantially justified.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The legal dispute in Ekman is governed by the interplay of several provisions of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (26 U.S.C.) and the Treasury Regulations (26 C.F.R.) promulgated thereunder. Under the statutory framework applicable to the tax year at issue, IRC § 174(a) permits a taxpayer to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year in connection with a trade or business as current expenses not chargeable to a capital account. However, IRC § 174(c) establishes an express statutory exclusion for land and depreciable property, providing that § 174 shall not apply to any expenditure for the acquisition or improvement of property to be used in connection with the research or experimentation and of a character which is subject to the allowance under IRC § 167 (relating to the allowance for depreciation) or IRC § 611 (relating to depletion). For such property, only the annual depreciation allowances computed under § 167 may be treated as § 174 expenditures.

Implementing IRC § 174(c), Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(4) mandates the strict segregation of capital asset costs from research expenses. Specifically, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1) dictates that expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of property subject to an allowance for depreciation under § 167 are not deductible under § 174, regardless of whether the property is used by the taxpayer directly in connection with research or experimentation. Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4) illustrates this rule through a mandatory allocation example in which a taxpayer expends $30,000 to develop a new machine for business use, where $10,000 represents the actual cost of materials and labor to construct the physical machine and $20,000 represents research costs not attributable to the machine itself; under § 174(a), only the $20,000 is deductible as an expense not chargeable to a capital account, while the $10,000 must be charged to the capital asset account. To determine whether tangible property is depreciable in the first instance, IRC § 167(a) authorizes as a depreciation deduction a reasonable allowance for the exhaustion, wear and tear, and obsolescence of property used in a trade or business or held for the production of income, and Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-2 clarifies that this depreciation allowance applies to that part of the tangible property which is subject to wear and tear, decay or decline from natural causes, exhaustion, and obsolescence.

While Ekman directly adjudicated a deduction under IRC § 174 and did not address the Research Credit, the ruling has been frequently cited by the IRS in disputes concerning the Research Credit under IRC § 41. Under IRC § 41(b)(1) and (2), Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) encompass in-house wages paid to employees for qualified services, 65% of contract research expenses paid to non-employees, and amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) define the term "supplies" as any tangible property used in the conduct of qualified research other than land or improvements to land, and "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation". Because § 41(b)(2)(C) uses the phrase "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation," which closely parallels the "of a character which is subject to the allowance under section 167" language of § 174(c), the IRS has applied Ekman in determining whether tangible test articles, prototypes, and tooling qualify as creditable supplies under § 41. Furthermore, where tangible research equipment is depreciable, IRC § 179 allows taxpayers to elect to treat the cost of qualifying depreciable business property as an immediate expense rather than a capital expenditure; for the 1991 tax year at issue in Ekman, IRC § 179(c)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.179-5(a) required the taxpayer to make the election on its return for the year the property was placed in service, although under current law (IRC § 179(c)(2), as made permanent by the PATH Act of 2015, and Rev. Proc. 2017-33) a § 179 election may be made or revoked on an amended return without the Commissioner's consent. Finally, in tax controversies resulting in litigation, IRC § 7430 permits a prevailing party to recover reasonable litigation costs and attorney's fees; under the version of IRC § 7430 and Tax Court Rule 232(e) applied in Ekman, the taxpayer seeking an award bore the burden of proof to establish that the position of the United States was not "substantially justified"—meaning that the government's position was not justified to a degree that could satisfy a reasonable person or lacked a reasonable basis in both law and fact—although for proceedings commenced after July 30, 1996, the Taxpayer Bill of Rights 2 shifted to the government the burden of establishing that its position was substantially justified.
The Court's Final Holding

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the U.S. Tax Court's judgment in favor of the Commissioner in all respects. Evaluating the Tax Court's factual findings for clear error and its legal conclusions de novo, the Sixth Circuit held that the $7,000 Porsche 928 S4 engine was tangible property subject to wear and tear—even if subjected to excessive wear and tear during testing—and therefore constituted depreciable property under IRC § 167 whose acquisition cost was barred from current deduction by IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b). The court noted that the Ekmans did not challenge on appeal the Tax Court's finding that the engine's cost was not deductible under IRC § 179 because they had failed to elect that deduction on their 1991 return, and declined to reach the Commissioner's alternative argument under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)(vi) as unnecessary. Finally, reviewing the denial of litigation costs for abuse of discretion, the Sixth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's refusal to award $13,850 in costs and attorney's fees under IRC § 7430, concluding that the taxpayers had failed to show that the Tax Court abused its discretion in finding that the Commissioner's position—both as to the deductions initially disallowed and later conceded after documentation was produced, and as to the $7,000 engine, on which the Commissioner prevailed—was substantially justified.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous forensic examination of the Ekman opinion reveals five distinct legal, evidentiary, procedural, and accounting failures that doomed the taxpayer's claim and prevented recovery of litigation costs. Each failure carries profound second- and third-order implications for corporate taxpayers structuring R&D tax credit claims under IRC § 41 and specified research or experimental expenditure treatments under IRC § 174.
Misconstruction of Statutory Character of Property Versus Intended Use

The primary legal failure committed by the taxpayers in Ekman was advancing a flawed teleological interpretation of IRC § 167 and § 174(c). On appeal, the Ekmans argued that the statutory allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167 presupposes an asset deployed in a trade or business to produce final goods or directly generate commercial revenue. Because Leonard Ekman used the $7,000 Porsche engine solely as a laboratory testbed to evaluate performance modifications—and never intended to sell the modified engine itself or use it to manufacture commercial inventory—the taxpayers asserted that the engine fell outside the ambit of § 167 and was consequently exempt from the depreciable property exclusion of § 174(c).

Both the Tax Court and the Sixth Circuit dismantled this legal theory, establishing the black-letter principle that eligibility under IRC § 174(c) hinges on the inherent nature or character of the property rather than its subjective intended use in research. As the Sixth Circuit emphasized by quoting IRC § 174(c), the statute expressly bars acquisition deductions for property "to be used in connection with the research or experimentation and of a character which is subject to the allowance under section 167". The Sixth Circuit held that the clear import of these provisions is that the character of the property, not the use of the property, determines whether an expense is deductible or only depreciable; indeed, because § 174(c) by its terms addresses property used in connection with research, treating research-only use as removing an asset from the class of depreciable property would leave the statutory exclusion with little or no effect. By conflating functional deployment in R&D with the intrinsic physical character of the asset, the taxpayers failed to recognize that an automobile engine is intrinsically a durable, multi-year mechanical asset subject to physical exhaustion and wear and tear.
Evidentiary Contradiction: Blowing Up the Engine Versus Excessive Wear and Tear

To circumvent the "character subject to depreciation" standard of Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-2, the taxpayers attempted a factual pivot on appeal, arguing that the Porsche engine was not depreciable property because it was "not subject to wear and tear, but is intentionally being destroyed as part of the on-going research". Specifically, while there was some indication in the record that Ekman had purchased the damaged 928 S4 engine with the intention of "blowing it up," the taxpayers contended that the engine was being intentionally destroyed as part of the ongoing research—which, on their theory, would render the engine a single-use, consumable R&D supply rather than a durable asset.
This argument failed on the merits because of a devastating evidentiary self-contradiction, even though the Commissioner's attempt to add a procedural bar was rejected.

First, from a procedural standpoint, the Commissioner invoked the doctrine of judicial estoppel (citing Griffith v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 135 F.3d 376, 380 (6th Cir. 1998)), arguing that the Ekmans were barred from disputing on appeal that the cost was subject to depreciation because they had taken that position in the Tax Court; the Sixth Circuit rejected this argument, observing that the taxpayers had argued in the Tax Court that the cost was deductible, but if not, then depreciable, so that judicial estoppel was not appropriate.

Second, and decisively on the merits, Leonard Ekman's own sworn trial testimony directly refuted his appellate characterization of destructive consumption. Under examination in the Tax Court, Ekman admitted that the $7,000 engine acquired in 1991 was modified, repaired, and still running five years later. Explaining what he meant by "blowing" the engine, Ekman testified that he meant some internal damage, stopping short of actually destroying the engine, after which the engine would be taken apart, examined for wear, and repaired. The Tax Court and the Sixth Circuit seized upon this testimony to formulate a critical evidentiary distinction: an asset that suffers internal mechanical damage during rigorous testing, is disassembled for inspection, is repaired, and remains operational years later is not consumed or destroyed. Instead, it is merely subjected to "wear and tear, even excessive wear and tear," which confirms rather than negates its status as a depreciable capital asset under IRC § 167(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-2.
Cost Accounting Failure to Segregate Capital Testbeds from Experimental Modifications

A related technical accounting lesson in Ekman concerns the distinction between the acquisition cost of the underlying test platform and the experimental costs of developing and testing specific component modifications, which Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(2) and (b)(4) treat differently. On their 1991 tax return, the Ekmans claimed Schedule C deductions both for the $7,000 purchase price of the existing Porsche 928 S4 engine and for the separately identified expenses of cam development, piston development, engine block development, and cylinder head development; the Commissioner ultimately allowed all of the development expenses, so the dispute concerned only the character of the $7,000 engine cost.

The regulatory example in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4)—quoted by the Tax Court and the Commissioner and reproduced by the Sixth Circuit in a footnote—provides that when a taxpayer develops a new machine ($30,000 total outlay), the research costs not attributable to the machine itself ($20,000) are deductible under § 174(a), whereas the actual costs of material, labor, etc., to construct the machine itself ($10,000) must be charged to the asset account. In Ekman's engineering project, the experimental uncertainty did not lie in whether a factory Porsche 928 S4 engine could operate at 130 to 150 mph—Porsche AG had already designed and manufactured that base engine. Rather, the experimentation resided in the custom-engineered camshafts, pistons, and cylinder heads designed to elevate horsepower for racing applications. By purchasing a pre-existing, manufactured engine to serve as a reusable test mule, Ekman acquired a capital testbed and potentially triggered Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)(vi) as the non-deductible acquisition of "another's patent, model, production or process". While the IRS conceded the deductibility of the component development expenses prior to trial, the Tax Court held that the $7,000 paid for the base testbed was the cost of an asset of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation, used in connection with research or experimentation, and therefore not deductible as a research or experimental expense under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(4).
Procedural Forfeiture of IRC Section 179 Expensing Elections

When confronted with the disallowance of the $7,000 engine under IRC § 174(c), the taxpayers attempted during Tax Court litigation to recharacterize the expenditure as an immediately deductible small-business asset expense under IRC § 179. However, deductions are a matter of legislative grace under New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering, 292 U.S. 435, 440 (1934), requiring strict compliance with statutory mechanics. Under IRC § 179(c)(1) and the regulations applicable to the 1991 tax year (Treas. Reg. § 1.179-5(a)), the § 179 election had to be made on the taxpayer's return, specifying the items of property to which it applied, so a taxpayer could not claim § 179 expensing for the first time during an audit or Tax Court trial; the later rules permitting a § 179 election to be made or revoked on an amended return without the Commissioner's consent did not apply to 1991. Because the Ekmans failed to elect a § 179 deduction for the engine on their 1991 return, the Tax Court found that its cost was not deductible under § 179—a finding the taxpayers did not challenge on appeal.
Pre-Trial Substantiation Deficiencies and the IRC Section 7430 Fee Recovery Trap

The final failure in Ekman highlights a costly procedural reality in federal tax litigation: winning 90% of a disputed R&D tax deficiency prior to trial does not guarantee recovery of legal fees under IRC § 7430. The Ekmans sought $13,850 in litigation costs and attorney's fees after the Commissioner, whose November 4, 1994 notice of deficiency had disallowed all of the disputed 1991 Schedule C deductions—including the camshaft, piston, engine block, and cylinder head development costs—conceded all of those expenses except the $7,000 engine before trial, reducing the asserted $2,929 deficiency to $307.

Under IRC § 7430 and Tax Court Rule 232(e), as applied in Ekman, the party seeking litigation costs bears the burden of proving that the Commissioner's administrative and litigation positions were not "substantially justified". In Ekman, the Tax Court found no evidence that the Commissioner's position in issuing the notice of deficiency was unreasonable, noting that the only evidence on the point was the Commissioner's statement that the adjustments were conceded after documentation was produced at a meeting with the taxpayers' counsel and accountant; the Sixth Circuit's opinion does not indicate that the cost of the two used Porsche automobiles was among the disputed deductions. Once that documentation was produced, the Commissioner conceded the component development expenses, a sequence that did not, in the Tax Court's view, show the Commissioner's position to be unjustified. Because the taxpayers, who bore the burden of proof, presented no evidence that the Commissioner's position in issuing the notice was unreasonable—and because, on the remaining $7,000 engine issue, the Commissioner's position was not only substantially justified but sustained by the court—the Sixth Circuit held that the taxpayers had failed to show that the Tax Court abused its discretion in denying the $13,850 fee petition.
Broader Doctrinal Evolution: From Ekman to TG Missouri and the 2014 Final Regulations

Understanding the full technical impact of Ekman requires tracing how the IRS utilized the decision in subsequent IRC § 41 R&D tax credit disputes, and how later case law and Treasury Regulations refined its reach. Following 1999, IRS examination teams and IRS letter rulings commonly cited Ekman to challenge IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) supply QREs claimed for prototypes, pilot models, dies, and production molds, treating such items as property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. The IRS argued under Ekman that any tangible test article or tool that physically survived testing and possessed a useful life exceeding one year was per se "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation," even if built solely for R&D.

A subsequent judicial decision, later IRS litigation concessions, and regulatory rulemaking cabined this overbroad application of Ekman across two distinct analytical dimensions: economic ownership of wear-and-tear risk and regulatory pilot model safe harbors. First, in TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), the Tax Court—in a holding that undercut the IRS's broad reading of Ekman—held that production molds that an automobile parts manufacturer acquired from third-party toolmakers and sold to its customers were not property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation in the manufacturer's hands, because title to the molds passed to the customers, so that the mold costs were properly included as supply QREs under Section 41; in the later automotive tooling controversy TSK of America Inc. v. Commissioner, the IRS conceded the taxpayer's tooling QREs in 2018 by stipulated decision without a court opinion, and Shiloh Industries Inc. v. Commissioner was filed as a Tax Court petition raising similar tooling issues in 2018. In Ekman, by contrast, Leonard Ekman retained ownership of the Porsche engine and bore the economic exhaustion of the asset over its multi-year operational life. Second, the final Section 174 regulations issued by the Treasury Department on July 21, 2014 (T.D. 9680, amending Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2) clarified the definition of qualifying research and development expenditures with respect to pilot models and prototypes built during design or testing phases to verify that proposed designs function properly. Under these regulations, a pilot model—any representation or model of a product, including a component of a product, produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement—can give rise to Section 174 expenditures, and the ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product is not relevant to that determination; the regulations also clarify that the depreciable property rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1) and (b)(4) is an application of the general definition of research or experimental expenditures and should not be applied to exclude otherwise eligible expenditures. Crucially, the disallowance in Ekman remains distinguishable even under the modern regulatory framework, because Ekman did not construct a custom pilot model to resolve design uncertainty of the model itself, but rather acquired an existing commercial Porsche engine that remained running five years later as a durable, multi-year testbed.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement adjudicated in Ekman v. Commissioner against the specific deficiencies in the taxpayer's position and the governing standard of proof applied by the U.S. Tax Court and the Sixth Circuit.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Rationale

cells: Presumption of Correctness & General Deductibility Burden Tax Court Rule 142(a); Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111 (1933); New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering, 292 U.S. 435 (1934)

Claimed R&D deductions on the 1991 return for both component modifications and the $7,000 engine purchase, with the Commissioner conceding the component expenses only after documentation was produced at a meeting with the taxpayers' counsel and accountant.

Preponderance of the Evidence: The Commissioner's deficiency determinations are presumed correct. Because tax deductions are a matter of legislative grace, the taxpayer bears the burden of proving strict compliance with every specific statutory requirement.
Exclusion of Depreciable Property from R&D Deductions IRC § 174(a), § 174(c); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1) (and analogous IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) supply QRE exclusion)

Argued that IRC § 167 depreciation applies only to assets used to produce commercial goods or income directly, and that because the $7,000 Porsche engine was used solely for R&D testing and not for resale, it was exempt from § 174(c).

Objective "Character of Property" Standard (De Novo Legal Review): Eligibility under § 174(c) turns on the intrinsic character of the property, not its subjective intended use. Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1) bars acquisition deductions for depreciable property irrespective of whether the asset is used exclusively in R&D.
Definition of Depreciable Tangible Property ("Wear and Tear") IRC § 167(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-2

Contended on appeal that the engine was "not subject to wear and tear, but is intentionally being destroyed as part of the on-going research," pointing to indications that it was purchased with the intention of "blowing it up".

Clear Error Factual Review / Physical Endurance Test: Testimony established that "blowing up" meant internal damage that was disassembled, inspected, and repaired, and the engine was still running five years later. Suffering repairable internal damage constitutes "excessive wear and tear," proving depreciable asset status rather than supply consumption.
Segregation of Capital Asset Costs from Research Costs Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(2), (b)(4)

Deducted the $7,000 acquisition cost of the base Porsche 928 S4 engine (the durable testbed machine) as a research expense alongside the experimental costs of developing custom cams, pistons, cylinder heads, and block modifications, rather than charging it to a capital asset account.

Strict Cost Allocation Mandate: Per the regulatory example in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), research costs not attributable to the physical machine itself are deductible under § 174(a), but the actual costs to acquire or construct the underlying capital machine must be charged to the capital asset account.
Acquisition of Another's Production, Model, or Process Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)(vi)
Purchased a pre-existing, factory-manufactured Porsche 928 S4 four-valve engine from a third party rather than fabricating a custom, single-use experimental component from raw materials.

Alternative Regulatory Disqualification: While the Sixth Circuit did not need to reach this issue given its holding under § 174(c), the regulation explicitly excludes expenditures for acquiring another party's existing model, production, or process from qualifying as R&D.
Procedural Consistency Between Trial and Appeal Doctrine of Judicial Estoppel; Griffith v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 135 F.3d 376 (6th Cir. 1998)

Argued in the U.S. Tax Court that the $7,000 engine cost was deductible, but if not, then depreciable, and argued on appeal that the engine was non-depreciable; the Commissioner contended that this shift was barred by judicial estoppel.

Judicial Estoppel Rejected: Judicial estoppel forbids a party from taking a position inconsistent with one successfully and unequivocally asserted in a prior proceeding; because the taxpayers had argued depreciability only in the alternative, the Sixth Circuit held that judicial estoppel was not appropriate and decided the depreciability issue on the merits.
Election to Expense Depreciable Business Assets IRC § 179(a), § 179(c)(1); Treas. Reg. § 1.179-5(a)

Attempted in Tax Court to claim an immediate expense deduction for the $7,000 engine under IRC § 179 after the IRS disallowed the § 174 deduction, despite never having elected § 179 on the 1991 tax return.

Mandatory Return Election Standard: Under the rules applicable to 1991, a taxpayer could not claim § 179 expensing in litigation without having made an election on the tax return specifying the items of § 179 property; the Tax Court found the engine cost not deductible under § 179 for lack of an election, and the taxpayers did not challenge that finding on appeal.
Recovery of Litigation Costs & Attorney's Fees IRC § 7430; Tax Court Rule 232(e)
Petitioned for $13,850 in attorney's fees and costs because the IRS conceded 90% of the assessed deficiency (the component modification costs) prior to trial.

Abuse of Discretion / "Substantially Justified" Standard: The taxpayer bears the burden under Rule 232(e) to prove the IRS's position lacked a reasonable basis in law and fact. The Tax Court found no evidence that the Commissioner's position in issuing the notice of deficiency was unreasonable—the adjustments were conceded after documentation was produced at a meeting with the taxpayers' counsel and accountant—and the Commissioner's position on the $7,000 engine was not only substantially justified but sustained at trial, so the taxpayers failed to show an abuse of discretion.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Ekman v. Commissioner into actionable tax planning and controversy defense, the following two industry case studies examine realistic corporate R&D projects confronting the exact legal, technical, and accounting pitfalls identified by the Sixth Circuit. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial blueprint across project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to satisfy both IRC § 41 (Research Credit) and IRC § 174 (Research and Experimental Expenditures).
Case Study 1: High-Performance Propulsion Engineering (Automotive Tier-1 Powertrain Developer)
Project Scenario and the Ekman Pitfall

Apex Powertrain Systems, Inc. ("Apex"), a United States Tier-1 automotive engineering firm based in Michigan (within the jurisdiction of the Sixth Circuit), initiates Project H2-Boost to develop a novel direct-injection hydrogen fuel rail, custom forged-titanium connecting rods, and a twin-scroll variable-geometry turbocharger system capable of retrofitting commercial heavy-duty diesel engines to run on zero-carbon hydrogen fuel without suffering hydrogen embrittlement or pre-ignition knock. To conduct dynamometer testing, Apex purchases four commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) heavy-duty 15-liter diesel engines from an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) for $60,000 each ($240,000 total). Over a 24-month testing campaign, Apex engineers install three successive iterations of custom-machined prototype injectors, pistons, cylinder head gaskets, and turbocharger housings ($380,000 in custom component fabrication costs) onto the four OEM engine blocks. During high-pressure dynamometer runs, extreme cylinder pressures crack several custom pistons and score the cylinder liners of the OEM blocks. After each failure, Apex technicians tear down the engines, hone and re-sleeve the OEM engine blocks, install the next iteration of custom prototype components, and resume testing. Three years later, three of the four OEM engine blocks remain mounted on Apex's dynamometer stands for ongoing testing.

On its federal income tax return, Apex's tax preparer aggregates the $240,000 COTS engine acquisition cost with the $380,000 custom prototype component cost, claiming the entire $620,000 as qualified "supplies used in the conduct of qualified research" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and as research expenditures under IRC § 174. Upon IRS examination, the IRS Engineering Team cites Ekman v. Commissioner, 184 F.3d 522 (6th Cir. 1999), and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4) to disallow the entire $620,000 supply QRE claim, asserting that Apex capitalized and commingled depreciable multi-year testbed engines ("still running" years later after repair of "excessive wear and tear") with unsegregated modification expenses.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Cost Accounting Restructuring

To eliminate the Ekman commingling trap under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), Apex must overhaul its enterprise resource planning (ERP) and project cost-accounting governance before procuring project hardware. Specifically, Apex must establish a dual-ledger Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) that enforces a hard accounting wall between capital testbeds and experimental components. Under this structure, WBS Account 100-CAP (Capital Testbed and Durables) captures the $240,000 acquisition cost of the four COTS 15-liter OEM base engines along with reusable dynamometer mounting rigs, whereas WBS Account 200-EXP (Experimental Pilot Models and Consumable Sub-Components) exclusively captures the $380,000 expended on custom-machined prototype hydrogen fuel rails, experimental titanium connecting rods, sacrificial cylinder head gaskets, and custom turbocharger impellers. In tandem with this ledger split, Apex's project charter must formally define the "business component" under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) not as the entire 15-liter engine, but specifically as the individual sub-assemblies (the hydrogen fuel-injection rail assembly, the connecting rod and piston assembly, and the turbocharger assembly). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), a component of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the appropriate design of that component qualifies as an eligible "pilot model" rather than a capital asset improvement. Finally, rather than erroneously claiming the $240,000 OEM base engines as § 41 supplies, Apex must capitalize the $240,000 into WBS Account 100-CAP and make a timely, affirmative election on its federal income tax return under IRC § 179(c)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.179-5 (an election that, under current law, may also be made on an amended return without the Commissioner's consent) to expense the engines immediately for income tax purposes (or claim applicable depreciation under IRC § 167). To the extent regular annual depreciation allowances under § 167 are taken on the four testbed engines while they are used directly in connection with R&D, Apex may include only those annual depreciation allowances as § 174 expenditures pursuant to IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1), while strictly excluding both the $240,000 acquisition cost and the depreciation allowances from IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) supply QREs.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Uncertainty Substantiation

To defeat any IRS contention under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)(vi) that Apex is merely acquiring or adapting "another's patent, model, production or process", and to prevent an initial broad-brush audit disallowance, Apex's lead propulsion engineers must draft a contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty Initialization Report prior to testing. This document must explicitly acknowledge that the OEM 15-liter diesel block is a known, commercially available baseline platform acquired solely as a mechanical host, while detailing the exact technological uncertainties inherent in the custom sub-components—specifically, that existing engineering data cannot establish the optimal injector nozzle geometry or titanium alloy grain structure required to prevent hydrogen auto-ignition and embrittlement at 300 bar injection pressure. Furthermore, by compiling itemized vendor invoices, CAD blueprints of the custom sub-components, and the WBS allocation schedule into a contemporaneous audit-ready binder at the time the tax return is filed, Apex ensures that if the IRS challenges the $380,000 sub-component QREs during examination, Apex can immediately rebut any claim that the government's disallowance has a reasonable basis in law and fact, thereby preserving Apex's ability to recover administrative and litigation costs under IRC § 7430 (under which, for proceedings commenced after July 30, 1996, the government bears the burden of establishing that its position was substantially justified) and Tax Court Rule 232(e).
Step 3: Contract Terms and Procurement Structuring

Apex must also restructure its vendor procurement contracts to establish an unmistakable legal distinction between capital equipment acquisitions and experimental prototype fabrication. Bundled purchase orders must be prohibited; the acquisition of the four COTS engines from the OEM must be executed under a standard Commercial Equipment Purchase Agreement, whereas the fabrication of the custom fuel rails, pistons, and turbochargers by third-party precision machine shops must be governed by a dedicated Custom Prototype and Experimental Supply Fabrication Agreement. The Statements of Work (SOWs) for the custom components must expressly stipulate that the parts are custom-engineered experimental pilot models fabricated to Apex's proprietary CAD specifications solely for developmental testing under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), and that they carry no commercial warranty of fitness or multi-year durability. Moreover, if any third-party vendor performs concurrent engineering or metallurgical testing on the custom parts, the contract must specify that Apex retains exclusive substantial rights to all resulting designs and bears the full financial risk of component failure by paying on a time-and-materials basis regardless of technical success, thereby qualifying eligible third-party engineering services as 65% Contract Research Expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and avoiding the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Physical Disposition Logs

To overcome the Sixth Circuit's "excessive wear and tear versus destruction" holding in Ekman, Apex must institute rigorous physical tracking of every experimental component from installation through final disposition. For each dynamometer run, engineers must record in an iterative hypothesis-testing log the specific technical hypothesis under evaluation, the empirical telemetry data collected, and the resulting structural degradation of the prototype sub-components. Crucially, unlike Leonard Ekman—who disassembled, repaired, and kept his engine running for five years—Apex must enforce a mandatory Experimental Supply Quarantine and Scrap Protocol for all items booked to WBS Account 200-EXP. When prototype injectors, titanium connecting rods, or cylinder heads are removed from the OEM testbed block after a test cycle, they must be subjected to destructive metallurgical cross-sectioning (such as scanning electron microscopy to measure internal hydrogen micro-cracking) or physically crushed and transferred to a certified scrap metal recycler. Each scrapped batch must be documented with a dated Certificate of Physical Destruction and Scrap Disposition signed by the laboratory director, proving conclusively that the $380,000 in custom components were physically consumed or destroyed during experimentation and possessed zero post-research useful life, fully satisfying IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4).
Case Study 2: Semiconductor Capital Equipment and Robotics Manufacturing (Wafer-Handling Pilot Model and Tooling Development)
Project Scenario and the Ekman Pitfall

VengaNano Robotics Corp. ("VengaNano"), a United States semiconductor equipment manufacturer, enters into a development program to engineer an ultra-high-vacuum (UHV) robotic wafer-transfer cluster tool for a major domestic microchip foundry ("Foundry Client"). The technical challenge requires developing a magnetically levitated (maglev) ceramic end-effector (the robotic arm assembly that grips silicon wafers) and a custom cryogenic thermal-isolation chamber capable of transferring 300mm extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography wafers at ultra-high vacuum without generating microscopic particle contamination or thermal warping. To build the developmental system in its cleanroom laboratory, VengaNano spends $1,500,000 acquiring two standard commercial cleanroom structural frames, high-vacuum roughing pumps, and generic multi-axis servo controllers from third-party industrial vendors. VengaNano then expends $950,000 in raw high-purity alumina ceramics, rare-earth neodymium magnets, custom-machined vacuum seals, and third-party fabrication labor to build three experimental iterations of the maglev end-effector and cryogenic chamber (the pilot models), plus $1,200,000 in internal R&D engineering wages. After 18 months of cleanroom testing—during which two ceramic end-effector prototypes shatter under thermal shock and the third pilot model successfully validates the design—VengaNano removes the custom cryogenic chamber, sells and transfers legal title of the validated custom chamber assembly to Foundry Client as contractually required prototype tooling, and retains the $1,500,000 structural frames, vacuum pumps, and servo controllers in its own cleanroom to serve as a permanent in-house R&D test bench for future product generations.

On its federal tax return, VengaNano claims the entire $2,450,000 hardware outlay ($1,500,000 base frames, pumps, and controllers plus $950,000 custom end-effectors and chamber) as qualified supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). During an IRS examination, the audit team cites Ekman v. Commissioner to disallow the entire $2,450,000 supply claim. The IRS argues that the $1,500,000 base frames, pumps, and controllers are durable, reusable testbed assets ("still running" in VengaNano's cleanroom) whose acquisition cost is barred by IRC § 174(c) and § 41(b)(2)(C), and that the $950,000 custom chamber and end-effector costs are inextricably commingled with the capital test bench under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Asset Classification Architecture

To insulate VengaNano's $950,000 pilot model and consumable outlays from disallowance while properly treating the $1,500,000 cleanroom test bench, VengaNano must institute a three-tier asset and supply governance policy aligned with Ekman, TG Missouri, and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). In the first tier, covering the retained multi-year R&D test bench, VengaNano must classify the $1,500,000 commercial cleanroom frames, vacuum roughing pumps, and servo controllers as capital R&D equipment on its Fixed Asset Ledger. Because VengaNano retains ownership of these items and uses them across multiple years (suffering normal or accelerated wear and tear under Ekman), their $1,500,000 acquisition cost is strictly excluded from IRC § 41 supply QREs and § 174 current deductions. Instead, VengaNano must make a timely election on its tax return under IRC § 179(c)(1) (an election that, under current law, may also be made on an amended return) or claim depreciation under IRC § 167, allocating only the annual § 167 depreciation allowance to its § 174 expenditure pool pursuant to IRC § 174(c). In the second tier, covering destroyed experimental pilot model components ($400,000 of the $950,000), the first two iterations of the custom maglev ceramic end-effectors that shattered or were consumed during thermal-shock testing are tracked in a dedicated Consumable R&D Supplies and Destroyed Pilot Models ledger, qualifying in full as IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) supply QREs and IRC § 174 expenditures. In the third tier, covering the customer-transferred pilot model and prototype tooling ($550,000 of the $950,000), the third custom cryogenic chamber and maglev end-effector iteration that survived testing and was sold to Foundry Client is tracked in a dedicated Customer-Delivered Prototype Tooling ledger; because VengaNano did not retain ownership of the asset and never claimed depreciation on it, this $550,000 falls squarely within the safe harbor of TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), securing full qualification as IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) supply QREs.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Component-Level Segregation

VengaNano must structure its engineering documentation to satisfy the strict cost allocation mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4) (the $30,000 machine example quoted by the Sixth Circuit in Ekman). To accomplish this, VengaNano's systems engineers and cost accountants must co-author a Master Experimental Bill of Materials (BOM) Segregation Schedule prior to assembly. This schedule maps every part number in the cluster tool assembly to either the non-qualifying host frame and pump infrastructure ($1,500,000) or the qualifying experimental sub-assemblies ($950,000). For every item on the qualifying $950,000 BOM, the engineering documentation must specify the exact design uncertainty being evaluated—such as magnetic flux decay and outgassing rates of the alumina maglev stator ring at cryogenic temperatures—directly satisfying the definition of a "pilot model" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) and proving that the $950,000 represents experimental costs rather than the capital construction of a business machine under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4).
Step 3: Contract Terms and Economic Risk Allocation

To ensure the $550,000 validated chamber and end-effector transferred to Foundry Client are neither disqualified as depreciable property under Ekman nor excluded as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), VengaNano must draft its commercial agreement with Foundry Client with surgical precision. First, to negate depreciable character under TG Missouri, the contract must explicitly state that legal title and physical possession of the validated prototype cryogenic chamber and maglev end-effector transfer to Foundry Client upon final acceptance testing, and that VengaNano retains no ownership interest in the physical unit thereafter. Under the holding of TG Missouri, because Foundry Client—not VengaNano—will suffer the economic loss from subsequent wear, tear, and obsolescence during commercial wafer fabrication, the $550,000 prototype is legally not "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" in VengaNano's hands, completely neutralizing the IRS's Ekman argument. Second, to satisfy IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), the contract must stipulate that Foundry Client's payment for the $550,000 prototype unit is strictly contingent upon the unit passing rigorous UHV cleanroom acceptance specifications (placing full financial risk of technical failure on VengaNano), and that VengaNano retains exclusive ownership and substantial rights to all underlying patents, maglev control algorithms, and manufacturing know-how developed during the project, granting Foundry Client only a non-exclusive license to use the delivered physical unit.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Post-Research Lifecycle Controls

To prevent the IRS from asserting at audit or trial that VengaNano's experimental components merely experienced "excessive wear and tear" while remaining available for internal use, VengaNano must implement end-to-end physical lifecycle controls. Every design iteration of the maglev end-effector and cryogenic seals must be tracked via sequential cleanroom Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) linked directly to employee timecards (substantiating the $1,200,000 in direct engineering wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)) and empirical vacuum test telemetry. For the $400,000 in shattered or failed ceramic prototypes, VengaNano must maintain cleanroom disposal manifests and photographic failure records proving irreversible physical destruction during testing. For the $550,000 validated pilot model, VengaNano must archive the signed customer bill of lading, title transfer certificate, and formal customer acceptance sign-off, proving that the physical unit permanently exited VengaNano's facility upon completion of R&D and was never placed in service as a depreciable asset by VengaNano. Finally, for the $1,500,000 retained cleanroom frame and pump test bench, VengaNano's fixed asset register must clearly reflect its placement in service as a capitalized asset under IRC § 167, demonstrating transparent statutory compliance and eliminating any basis for an IRS deficiency notice or accuracy-related penalty.
5. Synthesis of Practice Takeaways for U.S. Tax Advisors

The Sixth Circuit's ruling in Ekman v. Commissioner endures as a vital cautionary precedent for United States tax attorneys, certified public accountants, and corporate R&D tax advisors. First, practitioners must never rely on the subjective purpose or exclusive R&D deployment of a tangible asset to claim its acquisition cost as a deductible R&D supply or expenditure; if the physical item is intrinsically durable and survives testing through the repair of "excessive wear and tear," IRC § 174(c) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) mandate capitalization. Second, strict cost-accounting segregation under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4) and the 2014 pilot model rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) is essential to separate non-qualifying multi-year testbeds from qualifying experimental sub-components and pilot models. Third, taxpayers acquiring durable R&D test equipment must make timely, affirmative elections under IRC § 179 (or utilize regular depreciation under IRC § 167) on their returns rather than risking procedural forfeiture by misclassifying capital assets as R&D supplies, as the Ekmans did by failing to elect § 179 on their 1991 return. Finally, maintaining granular, audit-ready documentation prior to filing is the only reliable mechanism to prevent broad protective IRS deficiency notices and to establish that any subsequent government disallowance lacks substantial justification under IRC § 7430.

metaDescription: Ekman v. Commissioner (6th Cir. 1999): the cost of depreciable property, such as a research-use Porsche engine, is not deductible under IRC § 174(c).
